items.title: Arm Care: Rest, Recovery, and Pitch Counts
items.objective: The player will be able to explain why pitch counts and rest days exist, track their own throwing days, and tell an adult right away about any arm pain, tiredness, or soreness.
items.summary: Your arm is the only one you get. Learn why leagues count pitches and require rest days, how to keep track of your own throwing, and what to do if your arm hurts: tell an adult, every time.

video.note: A coach and a twelve-year-old looking at a pitch count log together, counting rest days on a calendar, and role-playing the player saying 'my arm feels sore' and the coach responding with 'thanks for telling me, you're done for today.'

explanation: A young arm is still growing. The bones in a child's elbow and shoulder have soft growth areas that adult arms do not have, and every hard throw puts stress on them. A little stress with rest in between makes the arm stronger. Too much stress with too little rest is how young players end up unable to throw for months. That is why pitch counts and rest days exist: not to hold you back, but to keep you playing.

A pitch count is the number of pitches a pitcher throws in a game. Little League sets a maximum number of pitches per day for each age, and the more pitches you throw in a day, the more days of rest you must take before pitching again. Those limits change over time and can differ by division, so GamePlanIQ uses the pitch-count table your league has configured, and your league follows the current Little League rulebook. If something on GamePlanIQ and your league's rulebook ever disagree, the rulebook wins. Ask your coach to show you the table.

Pitch counts only cover pitching, but your arm counts everything. Catching a full game, taking fifty throws of infield, playing catch at home, and long toss all add up. A good rule is one throwing-heavy day followed by a lighter day. Many leagues and medical groups also recommend taking at least a couple of months off from overhead throwing every year and not pitching for more than one team at a time. Check your league's current rulebook and ask your coach what they recommend for your age.

Recovery is what you do between throwing days. Sleep, water, a real cool-down after throwing, and easy movement like jogging and light stretching all help the arm bounce back. Ice packs are something some coaches use after pitching; follow your league's and your family's guidance on that. What never helps is throwing more to 'work through' a tired arm.

Here is the most important part of this lesson. If your arm hurts, feels tired in a new way, tingles, or just does not feel right, stop throwing and tell a parent or coach right away. That is not being weak; it is being a good teammate, because a player who speaks up today is a player who can pitch next month. GamePlanIQ cannot tell you what is wrong with your arm, and neither can your coach. Only a doctor can do that. The adults' job is to listen, stop the throwing for the day, and decide with your family whether a doctor should take a look.
parentInstructions: Learn your league's pitch-count and rest-day rules. GamePlanIQ shows the table your league has configured, but the league's current Little League rulebook is the official source. Ask the coach or league official if anything is unclear.

Keep a simple throwing log on the fridge or in your phone: the date, what your child did (pitched, caught, played catch, long toss), and roughly how many throws. Patterns of too many heavy days in a row are easy to see on paper and hard to see in the moment.

Make 'my arm hurts' a safe sentence in your house. Respond with thanks, stop throwing for the day, and never with disappointment. If pain lasts beyond the day, keeps coming back, or your child favors the arm, call your doctor. Do not diagnose it yourself and do not rely on the internet or GamePlanIQ to tell you what it is.

Watch for quiet signs of a tired arm: throws losing accuracy late in a session, a dropping elbow, rubbing the shoulder or elbow, or asking to stop. Those are your cue to end the throwing portion, not to push for 'a few more.'
If your child plays on more than one team, tell every coach. Pitch counts and rest days only work when every adult knows the whole picture.
Build the off-season into the year. A few months without overhead throwing, filled with other sports or activities, is widely recommended for young players and gives the arm a real break.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: This lesson needs no equipment. Use a calendar, a notebook, or the GamePlanIQ log to track throwing days and rest days.
steps: With a parent or coach, find your league's pitch-count table on GamePlanIQ and in the league's current rulebook. Write down your age group's daily maximum and the rest days required.
Count back through the last week together and write down each day you threw and roughly how much: pitched, caught, infield, catch at home, long toss.
Circle any stretch of three heavy throwing days in a row. Talk about which day could have been a light or rest day.
Practice the sentence out loud: 'Coach, my arm feels sore.' Have the adult practice the answer: 'Thanks for telling me. You're done throwing today.'
Make a list of three things you will do on a rest day that help your arm: sleep, water, easy movement, a different activity.
Do the arm care cool-down drill together after today's practice so you know how it feels.
Set a reminder to update your throwing log after every practice and game this week.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking only pitches count toward a tired arm.
commonMistakes.fix: Log every kind of throwing: catching, infield, catch at home, long toss. Plan one heavy day, then a lighter one.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hiding soreness to stay in the game or avoid letting the team down.
commonMistakes.fix: Speaking up is the team play. A player who rests today pitches next week; a player who hides it may miss the season.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pitching for two teams without each coach knowing the full count.
commonMistakes.fix: Parents tell every coach about every outing. The rest-day rule applies to the player, not the team.

commonMistakes.mistake: Throwing more to 'loosen up' a tired or sore arm.
commonMistakes.fix: Stop throwing for the day and tell an adult. If it lasts beyond the day or keeps returning, the family calls a doctor.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating the GamePlanIQ table as the rulebook.
commonMistakes.fix: GamePlanIQ shows what the league configured; the league's current Little League rulebook is official and wins any disagreement.

cues: Sore means stop and say so
safety: This lesson gives no medical advice. Any arm pain, swelling, numbness, or soreness that lasts beyond the day should be discussed with a doctor, not diagnosed by a coach, parent, or GamePlanIQ.
Follow your league's configured pitch-count and rest-day rules exactly, and check the league's current Little League rulebook because limits can change by year and division.
A player should stop throwing for the day whenever the arm hurts, and the adults should support that choice without pressure.

progression.easier: For 9- and 10-year-olds, keep it to two ideas: everything you throw counts, and if it hurts, stop and tell a grown-up. Make the throwing log a sticker chart.
progression.harder: For 13- to 16-year-olds, plan a full week: pitching day, rest days, a long-toss day, and lighter catch days, matched against the league table and the team schedule.

items.title: Throwing on the Run and Off-Balance Throws
items.objective: The player will be able to field a slow roller or a ball to the glove side while moving and make an accurate throw without stopping, using small steps to keep the body under control.
items.summary: Not every play lets you set your feet. Learn how to throw while moving, how to stay under control when you cannot, and when the smart play is to hold the ball.

video.note: A third baseman charging a slow roller, fielding it with the bare hand, and throwing on the run across the body; then a second baseman fielding on the move toward first and flipping underhand, each shown at full speed and in slow motion.

explanation: Everything you have learned so far assumes you have time to set your feet. In a real game, a slow roller or a ball hit to your glove side sometimes gives you no time at all. Advanced infielders learn to throw while still moving, and they learn it one step at a time, starting slow.

The first rule of throwing on the run is to keep your feet under you. Small, quick steps keep your head still and your eyes on the target. Long, leaping steps feel fast but throw your body off and send the ball wild. Run through the ball, not at it, so that your momentum is already going toward the target when you field it.

On a slow roller, a right-handed third baseman charges, fields the ball off the outside of the glove-side foot (or with the bare hand if it has stopped rolling), and throws on the next step with the throwing-side foot planted. The arm stays over the top as much as possible. A lower arm slot is sometimes needed on a very quick play, but it should be a choice for that play, not a habit. The throw will not be as hard as a set-feet throw, so pick a lower target and let the ball get there.

When you are moving toward first base and are very close to it, an underhand flip or a short dart is safer than a full throw. Keep the ball visible to the receiver, flip it firm and chest-high, and keep moving after the flip. If you are moving away from your target, the odds of an accurate throw drop fast; a smart player eats the ball, meaning holds it, instead of risking an error that gives the runner an extra base.

Off-balance throwing adds stress to the arm because the legs cannot help as much. That is why this lesson is for ages 11 and up, why reps are limited, and why most of the practice happens at jog speed. Game speed is the last thing you add, not the first.
parentInstructions: This is an advanced lesson. Your child should already have a smooth arm circle, a straight step, and clean footwork before trying it, and should warm up fully first.

Set a cone where a slow roller might stop, about 20 feet in front of your child, and stand at 'first base' 40 to 50 feet away with a glove. Roll the ball slowly so it is barely moving when your child reaches it.
Start at a walk, then a jog. Say 'small steps' every time the steps get long. Only after ten controlled throws at jog speed should the drill go to full speed.
Watch the head. If it is bouncing or the eyes leave the target, the steps are too big or the child is rushing. Slow it back down.
Teach the 'eat it' decision: have your child call 'throw' or 'hold' as they field the ball based on whether they are moving toward you. Praise a smart hold as much as a good throw.
Keep this to 15 to 20 throws. These throws are harder on the arm than set-feet throws, so this lesson should not be on a day with pitching or long toss.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Practice the footwork with no ball: jog toward a cone, pretend to scoop at the glove-side foot, and shadow throw on the next step. Outdoors with a tennis ball, roll it slowly yourself and throw to a wall target at half effort.
steps: Complete the full warm-up routine. Set a cone 20 feet in front of you and have your partner at 'first base' 40 to 50 feet away.
Walk through the footwork with no ball: approach the cone, scoop at the glove-side foot, plant the throwing-side foot, throw on the next step. Five reps.
Partner rolls a very slow ball. Jog to it with small steps, field it with the glove or bare hand, and throw to the partner's chest on the next step.
Repeat ten times at jog speed, calling out 'throw' or 'hold' based on whether your momentum is toward the partner.
Move to 'running toward first': start 30 feet from the partner, field a rolled ball while moving toward them, and flip underhand chest-high from 15 feet, continuing to move after the flip.
Finish with five slow-roller throws at game speed, only if the jog-speed throws were accurate.
Total about 15 to 20 throws. End with five easy set-feet throws from 40 feet.

commonMistakes.mistake: Long, leaping steps that bounce the head and spray the throw.
commonMistakes.fix: Small, quick steps. Run through the ball so your momentum already points at the target.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dropping to a sidearm slot on every running throw.
commonMistakes.fix: Stay over the top as much as the play allows. A low slot is a choice for one play, not a new habit.

commonMistakes.mistake: Throwing while moving away from the target and making an error.
commonMistakes.fix: Call 'hold' when momentum is wrong. Eating the ball is a good play.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to throw as hard as a set-feet throw.
commonMistakes.fix: Pick a lower target and let the ball get there. Accuracy beats velocity on the run.

commonMistakes.mistake: Going to full speed before jog-speed throws are accurate.
commonMistakes.fix: Ten controlled jog-speed throws earn five game-speed throws.

cues: Scoop at the front foot, throw on the next step
safety: Ages 11 and up only, after a full warm-up, and never on a day with pitching or long toss. Limit to 15 to 20 throws because off-balance throws load the arm more than set-feet throws.
Practice on dry, even grass or dirt. Running throws on wet grass or uneven ground can cause slips and falls.
The receiver wears a glove and stands still with a clear target; running throws arrive from odd angles.

progression.easier: Walk-speed only, with the ball already stopped at the cone. Focus on scooping at the front foot and throwing on the next step.
progression.harder: Add a live runner timing the play (with a soft ball), or add a backhand version where the player fields across the body and throws with a hop to re-balance.

items.title: Fixing Common Throwing Faults
items.objective: The player will be able to recognize four common throwing faults in themselves or a partner (sidearm or short-arm, stepping across the body, throwing off the back foot, and pushing the ball) and apply the matching fix and cue for each.
items.summary: Almost every wild or weak throw comes from one of four faults. Learn to spot them, understand why they happen, and use one simple fix and one short cue for each.

video.note: Split-screen demonstrations of each fault beside its corrected version: a dropped-elbow sidearm throw next to an L-position throw, a step across the body next to a chalk-line step, a back-foot throw next to a front-leg finish, and a pushed ball next to a thumb-down whip.

explanation: Coaches see the same four throwing faults on every field. The good news is that each one has a cause you can feel, a fix you can practice at home without a ball, and a two- or three-word cue a partner can call out. This lesson is a repair guide. Find the fault, apply the fix, and say the cue until it sticks.

Fault one: sidearm and short-arm. The ball comes out from beside the hip or the hand goes straight from the glove to the ear with no circle, usually because the elbow dropped below the shoulder. The ball tails, sinks, and loses speed, and the shoulder takes extra strain. Fix: slow-motion arm circles in front of a mirror, freezing at the L with the elbow level with the shoulder, then towel snaps from the same L. Cue: 'thumb down, L up.'

Fault two: stepping across the body. The front foot lands on the throwing-arm side of the line to the target, so the hips lock and the player throws around their own body, usually missing to the arm side. Fix: draw a chalk line from the back foot to the target and put a marker just to the glove side of it where the front foot must land. Cue: 'open the gate' or 'step on the line.'

Fault three: throwing off the back foot. The player's weight never moves forward; they let go of the ball while leaning back, and the throw floats high and short. This often comes from rushing or from a tiny step. Fix: step-and-freeze reps where the player steps, pauses with the weight over a bent front knee, and then throws; the back foot must drag or lift at the finish. Cue: 'nose over your front knee' or 'finish over the front leg.'

Fault four: pushing the ball. The hand stays behind the ball with the elbow leading only a little, like a shot put, and the ball comes out slow with no snap. It usually happens when the arm circle is skipped or when a player tries to steer the ball to the target. Fix: towel drill and wrist-flip throws from one knee that make the fingers whip over the top of the ball, then full throws with a loud 'snap' finish at the opposite hip. Cue: 'snap it' or 'fingers over the top.'

Work on one fault at a time, and work on it without a ball first. A player trying to fix three things at once fixes none of them. Pick the one that shows up most, spend a week on it, and then move on.
parentInstructions: Film three throws from the side and three from behind with your phone, then watch them in slow motion with your child. You do not need to know baseball to compare the picture to the four faults in this lesson.

Elbow check: at the moment just before the throw, is the throwing elbow about even with the shoulder? If it is pointing at the ground, that is fault one. Say 'thumb down, L up' and do ten slow shadow circles together.

Step check: from behind, draw an imaginary line from the back foot to you. Does the front foot land across it? Chalk the line, put a marker on the glove side of it, and ask for ten steps onto the marker with no throw.

Weight check: after the throw, is your child leaning backward or standing on the back foot? Ask them to freeze after each throw; the nose should be over the front knee and the back heel should be off the ground.
Push check: does the throw look like a shot put, with no snap? Use a hand towel and have them snap it at your open hand held at chest height, ten times, then throw a sock ball with the same snap.
Pick one fault for the week. Twenty-five soft-ball throws per session is plenty; the rest can be shadow work and towel snaps, which teach the same thing with no load on the arm.
items.equipmentFreeAlternative: Everything in this lesson can be done with a hand towel, a chalk line, and a mirror or a parent's phone camera. No ball is needed to fix any of the four faults.
steps: Film or watch three throws from the side and three from behind. Decide with a partner which one fault shows up most.
For sidearm or short-arm: ten slow arm circles in front of a mirror, freezing at the L with the elbow level with the shoulder, then ten towel snaps from the L.
For stepping across: draw a chalk line to the target, place a marker just to the glove side of it, and make ten step-and-freeze reps landing on the marker with toes at the target.
For throwing off the back foot: ten step-pause-throw reps with a sock ball, freezing with the nose over a bent front knee before the throw and lifting the back heel at the finish.
For pushing the ball: ten wrist-flip throws from one knee at 10 feet so the fingers whip over the top, then ten towel snaps finishing at the opposite hip.
Make 15 to 20 soft-ball throws from 15 to 20 feet with a partner calling the cue for your fault before each throw.
Film three more throws and compare them to the first three. Write down the cue you will use this week.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to fix every fault in one session.
commonMistakes.fix: One fault per week. Pick the one that shows up most and ignore the rest for now.

commonMistakes.mistake: Doing all the repair work with full-speed throws.
commonMistakes.fix: Shadow circles, towel snaps, and step-and-freeze reps first. Live throws come last and stay soft.

commonMistakes.mistake: Cue overload: the parent says five things before each throw.
commonMistakes.fix: One cue, two or three words, said once. 'Thumb down, L up.' Then quiet.

commonMistakes.mistake: Only fixing the fault at 15 feet and losing it at game distance.
commonMistakes.fix: When the fix holds at 15 feet, move to 30, then 45, keeping the same cue. Film again at each distance.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a fault means the child is 'not a thrower.'
commonMistakes.fix: All four faults are habits, and habits change with two weeks of correct reps. Most players have one or two.

safety: Do the repair work without a ball or with a towel and sock ball. Live throws stay at about 25 per session and at soft-ball distance of 15 to 20 feet.
Fixing a fault can feel awkward and the arm may be used in a new way; stop for the day if anything hurts and tell a parent or coach.
Indoors or in a garage, use a towel or sock ball only and face a wall or net with nothing breakable nearby.

progression.easier: Work only on the arm circle with a towel and a mirror until 'thumb down, L up' looks right every time; the other faults often shrink once the elbow is up.
progression.harder: Have the player coach a younger sibling or teammate: spot the fault, name it, and give the cue. Teaching it proves they understand it.
